To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
T-cell activation and T-cell effector function is regulated by TCR-pHLA interactions and that TCR-pHLa affinity regulates the metabolic shift in T-cells.
TCR-pHLA binding affinity modulates the relative contributions of oxidative phosphorylation and glycolysis to TCR-dependent activation of CD4+ T-cell cytokine production and CD8+ cytotoxicity.

(1) T-cell receptor binding affinity modulates the relative contribution of glycolysis and oxidative phosphorylation in antigen specific CD4+ and (2) T-cell clones; (3) CD8+ T cells have a higher reliance on oxidative phosphorylation than CD4+ T cells for cytokine production.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of the immune system in the pathogenesis and treatment of human disease, and how the immune system can be harnessed to treat disease.
the role of the T-cell receptor in controlling T-cell metabolism.
understanding the role of metabolic adaptation in the function of T-cells, and the implications for the development of novel therapeutic strategies.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the metabolic pathways are regulated in a cell-type and antigen-specific manner.
metabolic adaptation of CD4+ T cells is more dependent on glycolysis, while the CD8+ T cells are more reliant on oxidative metabolism.
TCR-mediated stimulation of human CD4+ T-lymphocytes induces an adaptive metabolic shift to glycolytic metabolism and that this is not the case for CD8+ T cells.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the metabolic adaptation of human CD4+ T-cell to antigenic stimulation occurs through a glycolytic shift, while CD8+ T cells rely more on oxidative phosphorylation for cytokine production.
the metabolic adaptation of human T-cell clones is dependent on TCR–pMHC binding affinity and that the metabolic shift is different in CD4+ and in CD8+ human T-cells.

we have identified that the metabolic pathways that are used by CD4+ and CDB+ T-cells to generate the energy and biosynthetic precursors required for their effector function is controlled by the strength by which the T-cell receptor interacts with its cognate peptide-MHC complex.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the metabolic pathways utilized by T-cells are highly dependent on the nature and strength of the TCR-pHLA interaction.
metabolic adaptation is a critical feature of human T-cell activation and is controlled by TCR–pMHC affinity.
the strength of T-cell receptor ( TCR )-mediated activation is a key determinant of the metabolic shift in human T-cells.
